title: MorphServe: Efficient and Workload-Aware LLM Serving via Runtime Quantized Layer Swapping and KV Cache Resizing
one_line: An LLM serving runtime that, under memory pressure, asynchronously swaps selected FP16 decoder layers for pre-quantized INT4/INT8 copies and hands the reclaimed GPU memory to the paged KV allocator as extra cache blocks, reversing both when pressure subsides.

repo.evidence: Repo lives under the authors' lab org github.com/ds2-lab (Yue Cheng's group, UVA); repo/README.md:52-57 cites the paper with the correct author list and repo/README.md:43 links to the MLSys 2026 oral page; paper section 5 gives this exact URL as 'The source code is available at https://github.com/ds2-lab/MorphServe'. It is official, but it contains no code.
repo.badge_evidence: none found - MLSys does not operate an artifact-evaluation badge program, and neither the paper, the proceedings page, nor repo/README.md claims a badge

H1_open_repo.evidence: repo/ contains only LICENSE and README.md. repo/README.md:7-11 states verbatim: 'We are currently preparing the codebase for public release. The repository is being cleaned, documented, and organized for reproducibility... The full code will be released soon. Stay tuned!' repo_facts.json confirms file_count=2, size_mb=0.0, build_files=[], lines_by_extension={}. Paper section 5 says the system is ~2,200 lines of Python plus ~500 lines of C++/CUDA on top of SwiftLLM; none of it is present. Re-verified on github.com on 2026-09-14: still 2 files, no commits since 2026-04-21, 0 stars/forks/issues. Checked the whole ds2-lab org (ZipLLM, ELF, infinicache, Wukong, LambdaFS, NotebookOS, ALPS, FaaSNet) and searched the web for a mirror or fork: no implementation exists anywhere. This is exactly the 'code coming soon' placeholder the rubric excludes.

H2_no_root.evidence: Judged from the paper alone, since there is no code to read. Appendix C (p.18-19) describes only user-space CUDA: layer variants pinned in host DRAM, GEMM kernels precompiled on dummy data, in-place swaps via cudaMemcpyAsync into preallocated GPU regions, morphing and decoding on separate CUDA streams, and custom Triton kernels for KV block registration/remapping. Section 5 says it is built on SwiftLLM, a Python inference framework. No kernel module, eBPF, perf counter, KVM, hugepage, or /proc/sys requirement appears in sections 4, 5, or Appendix C. repo_facts.json red_flags is empty.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: Section 5 and Appendix C: the three 7B-8B models (Vicuna 7B v1.5, Llama 2 7B, Llama 3 8B) were evaluated on an NVIDIA L4 with 24 GB HBM and 256 GB DRAM - the same GPU memory as this machine's RTX A5000, and the A5000 (Ampere 8.6) is the faster part. The authors already downscale the Azure trace 4.75x and BurstGPT 1.75x specifically 'to fit our hardware environment' (section 5) and use short 512/256 and 1024/512 prompt/response lengths. Only CodeLlama 34B needs an A100 80 GB; dropping it is a clean scale-down that still covers both MHA and GQA. Host DRAM is the one gap (paper assumes 256 GB, this machine has 125 GB shared), but ~2x a 7B model in pinned FP16+W8+W4 copies is under 40 GB. The mechanism is INT4/INT8 weight-only, so the Ampere lack of FP8 kernels is irrelevant.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: Appendix C (p.19-20) gives public URLs for every input: Azure LLM Inference Dataset 2023 (github.com/Azure/AzurePublicDataset), BurstGPT (github.com/HPMLL/BurstGPT), GovReport (huggingface.co/datasets/launch/gov_report), QMSum (github.com/Yale-LILY/QMSum), DuReader (github.com/baidu/DuReader), Multi-News (github.com/Alex-Fabbri/Multi-News), Vicuna-7B-v1.5 (huggingface.co/lmsys/vicuna-7b-v1.5, ungated). AWQ INT4 checkpoints are publicly distributed and the base framework SwiftLLM (github.com/interestingLSY/swiftLLM) is public. Llama 2 7B and Llama 3 8B are license-gated on HF, which is friction rather than a blocker since ungated Vicuna 7B v1.5 is one of the paper's own four models. The only unobtainable dependency is MorphServe itself, which is H1's failure, not H4's.

reproduce.target: Figure 6 (p.9) - TTFT vs RPS on DuReader for Vicuna 7B v1.5 and Llama 2 7B, supporting the claim that MorphServe delays the saturation point and achieves 1.6x-1.83x higher throughput than FP16 serving. Chosen because it sweeps a scalar knob (RPS) rather than replaying a timestamped trace, so it needs no trace/dataset alignment machinery, and only requires the FP16 and static-AWQ-INT4 baselines, both off-the-shelf.
reproduce.scale_down: Drop CodeLlama 34B entirely (needs A100 80 GB). Keep Vicuna 7B v1.5 (ungated on HF) and, if the Llama license can be accepted, Llama 3 8B. Retain the authors' own 1.75x/4.75x trace downscaling and 512/256 (MHA) and 1024/512 (GQA) prompt/response lengths, which were already chosen for a 24 GB L4 and transfer unchanged to the 24 GB A5000. Use published AWQ INT4 checkpoints rather than re-quantizing. Reduce the RPS sweep to ~5 points bracketing the saturation knee.
reproduce.effort: As the repo stands today: 6-10 person-weeks of reimplementation (~2,700 LOC per section 5) before any reproduction can even be attempted, which consumes most of the 10-week budget. If the code were released as promised: ~8-12 person-days + ~30-50 GPU-hours on the A5000.
reproduce.rationale: Level L because there is nothing to reproduce. The rubric's M ('reproducible with real porting work') presupposes an artifact to port; here the first step is reimplementing the system from prose. The two components the paper itself calls the central challenges (Appendix C) - zero-overhead precision switching via weight-pointer redirection into preallocated GPU regions with precompiled per-precision GEMM dispatch, and custom Triton kernels that register non-contiguous reclaimed memory as PagedAttention blocks - have no pseudocode anywhere in the paper. The controller's thresholds are given only as illustrative examples (KV > 85%, queue delay > 100 ms, section 4.1); the three runtime modes (default/performance/accuracy) are named in section 5 but never parameterized; the hysteresis window length (section 6, Appendix D) is never quantified. Everything else about the paper is favourable - the hardware matches almost exactly (24 GB L4 vs 24 GB A5000), the traces are pre-downscaled by the authors, and every dataset and trace is public - which makes the missing artifact the sole, decisive obstacle.

addons.name: Predictive morphing from trace forecasting
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that replacing MorphServe's reactive threshold trigger with a short-horizon workload forecast reduces P95 TTFT and SLO-violation rate on the leading edge of a burst, under the BurstGPT and Azure LLM traces, compared with MorphServe's reactive controller, at equal or better average generation quality.
addons.mechanism: Add a forecaster to the Morphing Controller (section 4.1): an EWMA or small AR / gradient-boosted model over the last N seconds of (arrival rate, prompt-token volume, KV occupancy) that predicts KV occupancy H seconds ahead. Fire LayerSwapper when the predicted occupancy crosses the threshold, retaining the existing hysteresis as a fallback. The win is not swap latency (~6 ms per section 4.3) but eliminating the queue that accumulates while the reactive controller waits for pressure to persist across multiple consecutive forward passes (section 6, 'Stability under Oscillating Load'). Sweep the horizon H to expose the precision/recall tradeoff: over-eager forecasting quantizes layers that were never needed, paying accuracy for nothing.
addons.motivating_evidence: Appendix D, verbatim: 'MorphServe reacts to system pressure in real time but does not anticipate upcoming surges. Integrating lightweight workload forecasting could enable proactive morphing decisions and further improve responsiveness under bursty traffic.' Figure 1b shows TTFT already exceeding the 2 s SLO at the burst onset, which is precisely the interval a forecast would cover.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The forecaster is a few hundred lines and the evaluation reuses the existing trace-replay harness and the Figure 4/6 plots unchanged. Rated M on the assumption the code is released; against today's empty repo it is L, because the prerequisite is a full reimplementation of MorphServe.
addons.research_value_rationale: The authors explicitly name it as future work, so a reviewer would find it expected rather than surprising. It earns M rather than L because the negative result is genuinely informative: if 6 ms swaps mean reaction is already fast enough that forecasting buys nothing measurable, that cleanly falsifies the authors' own stated direction.

scoop_check.details: Searched 'proactive workload forecasting predictive precision adaptation LLM serving quantized layer swapping 2026' and 'papers citing MorphServe 2506.02006'. Forecast-driven LLM serving exists but at a different control knob: SageServe (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.14617) forecasts demand to drive cluster auto-scaling, and Predictive-LoRA (https://arxiv.org/html/2512.20210) uses an LSTM traffic predictor to prefetch LoRA adapters. Neither uses a forecast to drive weight-precision morphing. No paper citing MorphServe was found.

addons.name: Sub-layer morphing granularity (attention vs MLP)
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that morphing attention and MLP submodules independently, rather than whole decoder layers, achieves a strictly better accuracy-per-byte-freed frontier under the same memory-pressure schedule, compared with MorphServe's layer-granular swapping.
addons.mechanism: Split the LIS profiler (section 4.2, Algorithm 1 in Appendix A.2) so LTS/LRS/MDS are computed per submodule (self_attn.{q,k,v,o}_proj, mlp.{gate,up,down}_proj - the names appear in Figure 3e) instead of per layer, producing a ranked list of ~7xL entries. Extend the swapping sequence and the preallocated-GPU-region bookkeeping in LayerSwapper to submodule granularity. In a Llama-2-7B decoder layer the MLP is roughly twice the attention block, so submodule granularity gives both a finer memory quantum (~0.13 GB vs the paper's ~0.4 GB FP16 layer) and the option to quantize the insensitive half of a layer whose other half is sensitive.
addons.motivating_evidence: Appendix D, verbatim: 'MorphServe currently applies morphing at the transformer layer level. While effective, finer-grained adaptation, such as independently adjusting attention and MLP submodules, could unlock additional efficiency and precision flexibility.' Table 8 supplies the opening: LIS barely separates from a naive Front-to-Back order at layer granularity (Llama 2 7B, 16 layers swapped: 5.52 vs 5.54 PPL), and section A.3 admits MorphServe defaults to Front-to-Back when profiling is unavailable - suggesting the layer-level signal is nearly saturated and the remaining headroom lies below the layer.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The profiler change is small and entirely offline (section A.3: full LIS for a 32-layer model takes under 15 minutes on one GPU, so ~7x that is still trivial on the A5000). The runtime change is more invasive: the 'copy into the same memory addresses, no pointer remapping' invariant of section 4.3 assumes layer-sized regions, so the allocator bookkeeping must be reworked. Cross-cutting, hence M.
addons.research_value_rationale: Directly addresses a limitation the authors name, and the result transfers to any precision-switching serving system. Marked down from H because the likely outcome (finer granularity helps somewhat) is not surprising, and the flatness of Table 8 hints the effect size may be small.

scoop_check.details: Per-submodule and per-channel mixed-precision bit assignment is well-trodden in the static PTQ literature the paper itself cites (HAWQ, Risso et al. channel-wise mixed-precision assignment, AffineQuant). What appears unclaimed is doing it as a runtime, reversible knob inside a live serving loop with concurrent KV resizing. No follow-up work to MorphServe found.

addons.name: SSD-backed layer streaming instead of a 2x host-DRAM resident pool
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that streaming quantized layer variants from NVMe on demand, backed by a small pinned host-DRAM cache, holds P99 TPOT within a few percent of the fully-resident design while cutting host memory for layer variants by more than 2x, under the paper's Azure and BurstGPT traces.
addons.mechanism: Replace the 'all variants pinned in host DRAM' preloading of section 4.3 with a two-tier store: the top-k entries of the LIS swap sequence stay pinned in DRAM, the tail lives on NVMe and is read with O_DIRECT / io_uring into a pinned staging buffer and then DMA'd to the GPU. The paper's own numbers make this directly testable - a swap is ~6 ms end-to-end with ~4 ms of PCIe transfer for a ~0.1 GB INT4 Llama-2-7B layer - so the question is whether prefetch depth can hide the added NVMe read. Sweep k from 0 (pure streaming) to L (the paper's design) and report the memory/P99-TPOT frontier.
addons.motivating_evidence: Appendix D, verbatim: 'To support runtime layer swapping, MorphServe stores both full-precision and quantized variants in host memory. Although this increases memory usage, the overhead is typically under 2x the model size... Future work may further reduce this cost by streaming layers from SSD to host memory on demand or directly fetching them from SSD via GPUDirect Storage (GDS).' Section 6 separately lists 'demand-driven layer streaming' as an open item.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Fits this machine unusually well - 2x Samsung PM9A3 NVMe with ~257 GB free - and the experiment is about precisely the constraint this machine has that the paper's did not (125 GB shared DRAM vs the paper's 256 GB). GPUDirect Storage proper requires the nvidia-fs kernel module, which is not installable without root, so the design must use the ordinary read-then-DMA path; that is a real restriction but does not invalidate the hypothesis. Needs a new microbenchmark harness alongside the end-to-end one, hence M not H.
addons.research_value_rationale: Converts the paper's throwaway 'under 2x and serving clusters have plenty of DRAM' hand-wave into a measured tradeoff curve, and it is exactly the direction that would make MorphServe viable for the edge deployments section 6 says the authors care about. Not H because tiered weight streaming is a familiar systems pattern and reviewers would expect it to broadly work.

scoop_check.details: No work found that applies SSD-tiered variant storage to runtime precision switching. Weight streaming from SSD is standard for offloaded inference (FlexGen, DeepSpeed-Inference, ServerlessLLM - the last cited by the paper), but those stream a single precision's weights to fit a model that does not otherwise fit, not multiple precision variants of the same layer to support reversible morphing.

addons.name: Joint weight-precision and KV-precision morphing
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that adding KV-cache quantization as a third runtime knob, co-scheduled with layer swapping, sustains a higher request rate before saturation than weight-only morphing at matched end-to-end generation quality, under long-context workloads such as GovReport (2k+ token documents).
addons.mechanism: Add a KVQuantizer alongside KVResizer (section 4.4) that demotes cold KV blocks - those belonging to older positions of long-running sequences - from FP16 to INT8 in place, plus a joint policy in the Morphing Controller that chooses, per pressure event, between swapping another layer and demoting another tranche of KV blocks. The two knobs degrade quality along different axes: layer swapping costs accuracy on future tokens of all requests, KV demotion costs accuracy on past context of specific requests. Which is cheaper per byte freed, and whether the two compose or interfere, is the research content.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 6, verbatim: 'MorphServe can extend beyond weight-only quantization to include activation and KV quantization. Such extensions promise higher efficiency but raise calibration and scheduling challenges.' Section 4.4 is explicit that 'KVResizer does not quantize or compress existing KV caches' - the lever is simply unused. The paper's own comparison against PyramidKV (section 5.1) shows KV compression preserves accuracy but yields limited TTFT gains, which sets up the hybrid as the interesting middle ground.
addons.feasibility_rationale: INT8 KV quantization has mature open kernels to borrow and the evaluation reuses the existing harness, models, and datasets on a single 24 GB GPU. But mutating the paged block layout while KVResizer is concurrently attaching and detaching blocks is the most delicate part of the system - Appendix C already calls non-contiguous KV block management a central challenge - so this is a cross-cutting change well beyond a localized patch.
addons.research_value_rationale: The one add-on where either outcome teaches something non-obvious. The paper's entire thesis is that reversible, coordinated adaptation beats static compression; testing whether a second, qualitatively different knob composes with the first, or whether the two interfere because both degrade the same output tokens, is a genuine test of that thesis rather than an extension of it. A reviewer at MLSys would care about the answer either way.

scoop_check.details: KV quantization (KIVI, QServe W4A8KV4, Atom - the last two cited by the paper) and adaptive KV budgeting (PyramidKV, AdaKV, DynamicKV - all cited) are well covered as standalone static policies. The closest neighbour found is FineServe (https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.21081), on precision-aware KV slabs and two-level scheduling for heterogeneous-precision serving, but it schedules across models of fixed precision rather than co-morphing weight and KV precision for one model at runtime. No direct scoop.

addons.name: Per-request quality fairness under morphing
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that MorphServe's pressure-triggered morphing distributes accuracy degradation unevenly across requests - concentrating it on requests that happen to be decoding during a burst - and that a quality-budget-aware scheduling policy equalizes the per-request degradation distribution at negligible cost to P95 TTFT.
addons.mechanism: Two halves. First, measure: instrument the decode loop to tag each generated token with the active precision configuration, then report the distribution across requests of 'fraction of tokens generated under quantized layers', rather than only the aggregate F1/ROUGE-L the paper reports. Second, if that distribution is skewed, add a per-request quality budget to the scheduler: a request that has already exceeded its degraded-token budget gets priority for FP16 execution, or is deferred rather than degraded further.
addons.motivating_evidence: The paper reports only aggregate quality (Figure 4, Tables 4, 5, 9), and the mixed-precision study in Table 1 uses hand-constructed schedules ('First 1K FP16, Last 1K W4', etc.), not the distribution the real controller actually produces. Section 6's 'Fairness' paragraph argues fairness holds because continuous batching preserves FIFO and chunked prefill prevents starvation - but that is an argument about latency fairness and says nothing about quality fairness, the axis MorphServe newly introduces. Table 1 shows the schedule matters a great deal: 'First 1K FP16 / Last 1K W4' scores F1 16.61 while the reverse scores 14.71, a 13% spread at an identical count of quantized tokens.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The measurement half is pure instrumentation - a per-token precision tag plus a histogram - and reuses every existing workload, baseline, and trace unchanged. The policy half is a localized change to the scheduler. Comfortably within the 'few modules, existing harness, 2-4 students in 10 weeks' bar and well inside this machine's capacity, conditional on the code existing at all.
addons.research_value_rationale: It identifies a metric the paper does not report and whose absence is load-bearing for its central claim of improving latency 'without compromising generation quality'. A per-request tail-quality metric is the natural analogue of tail latency, and Table 1's 13% schedule-dependent spread suggests the tail is real. Either result is informative: a flat distribution vindicates the design under a sharper lens, a skewed one exposes a fairness problem the paper explicitly claimed not to have.

scoop_check.details: Searched for follow-ups citing MorphServe and for quality-fairness in mixed-precision serving; nothing found. Fairness in LLM serving is active (e.g. VTC, OSDI'24) but is framed entirely around throughput and latency share, not around degradation-quality share - an axis that only exists once weight precision becomes a runtime variable, which is new with this paper.

risks: DECISIVE: the artifact does not exist. repo/ holds only LICENSE and README.md; repo/README.md:7-11 says 'The full code will be released soon.' Paper section 5 describes ~2,200 lines of Python and ~500 lines of C++/CUDA on SwiftLLM, none of it published. Every H2/H3/H4 judgement in this audit rests on the paper text alone and is unverified.

No release date and no momentum. MLSys 2026 has already taken place; the repo was created and last pushed on 2026-04-21 and has had no commit in the ~5 months since, with 0 stars, 0 forks, and 0 issues. A team picking this paper would bet the semester on an event with no announced timeline and no fallback if it slips past week 3.

Reimplementation is not a viable Plan B. The two components the paper itself calls the central challenges (Appendix C) - in-place weight-pointer redirection with precompiled per-precision GEMM dispatch, and custom Triton kernels for dynamic non-contiguous KV block registration and index remapping - are described only in prose, with no pseudocode. The controller's thresholds are given as illustrative examples only (KV > 85%, queue delay > 100 ms), the three runtime modes are never parameterized, and the hysteresis window is never quantified.

No external reproducibility signal. MLSys runs no artifact-evaluation badge program, and neither the paper, the proceedings page, nor the README claims a badge, so there is nothing to fall back on in place of reading the code.

Host DRAM is tighter here than in the paper: section 5 used 256 GB, this machine has 125 GB shared with other users. Adequate for 7B/8B (~40 GB of pinned FP16+W8+W4 variants) but with no slack, and pinned memory cannot be swapped out.

Llama 2 7B and Llama 3 8B weights are license-gated on Hugging Face while env.md only guarantees non-gated HF access. Ungated Vicuna 7B v1.5 covers the MHA case so this is friction rather than a blocker, but it halves model coverage if the gate cannot be cleared.
CodeLlama 34B is out of reach (evaluated on A100 80 GB in section 5), so any reproduction covers at most 3 of the paper's 4 models and loses the largest-scale GQA data point.

Toolchain risk that cannot be checked without code: system nvcc is 11.8 while a SwiftLLM-class project likely needs CUDA 12.x. A conda-installed CUDA 12.1 toolkit is the route and driver 535 supports up to 12.2, but anything pinned to CUDA 12.4+ kernels would be a blocker.

Even the offline-profiling contribution is soft: Table 8 shows LIS is statistically indistinguishable from a naive Front-to-Back order across all four models, and section A.3 admits Front-to-Back is the default when profiling is unavailable. A reproduction aimed at the LIS contribution would be measuring a near-null effect; the value is concentrated in the runtime systems mechanisms, which are exactly the unreleased parts.
